doc.title: Phil Schaap interviewed by Monk Rowe, Toronto, Canada, January 9, 2003

title: Pay, union scale and pride in the West End
summary: Scale, union dues, star fees, and why the West End was a closed, positive chapter with his teachers.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Getting paid: wages, scale and the pay envelope

blocks.x: Can you recall what you were able to pay these jazz artists when you were—
Yeah I’m not proud of it but thankfully it was slightly above scale.
Scale was $55.65, which is an unusual small higher salary for the leader.

Yeah usually it’s double for the leader. But the scale, and also I paid the union dues. In fact I carved out that 802’s AF of M, although David Sheldon can verify this, although I’m not a member of the musician’s local, I was the delegate of the local 802 American Federal of Musicians for the address 2913 Broadway in Manhattan. Just for that address. And I went down to the union on Tuesdays and I think gave $28.45 every Tuesday. This is thirty years ago. And then the money got better. And of course certain acts — you know Jo Jones got more than that and Benny Carter — I shouldn’t be telling Mr. Carter’s salary, Benny Carter was getting a thousand dollars a night and a percentage. And Dizzy was getting a lump sum and he paid the band, and that would be more than a thousand then. I think scale by 1990, which would be the last year there was a formal scale, was $135.65. And we paid much more than that which is probably why it ended.

We did from ’84 on. And we went by minimum and bulk audience the first eleven years, which is a better system actually, for everybody. I mean the owners too. I mean there’s a reason why I worked the West End for 17 years. I made money for the owner. But it’s actually, you could see that I was a little awkward that the wages weren’t overly great, but I’m not embarrassed by them. But in a sense I’m most proud of the West End episode because it’s the only clear cut, well defined, start, middle and finish episode of my career in which the bottom line is so rosy in that the musicians who raised me were not old at the time that I started jazz at the West End. We are now in a position to appreciate that much better because they were largely in their late fifties, early sixties, late fifties. Jo Jones turned fifty, sixty rather, on October 7, 1971. So early sixties. Earle Warren was in his late fifties. He turned sixty on July 1, 1974. And so for the final stances of when they were not old, the last chapter of their career, they returned to the music that was their heart and played it in a very friendly atmosphere much nicer than most nightclubs, for reasonable money. And then they either died or retired. So the set concluded. It’s a closed set and a positive one.

It was great. And it actually created a different type of relationship for me with me original teachers. Because they were still teaching but it was different. And the day to day life with them may actually be my greatest jazz credential.
